title: Out of the depths
hook: a psalm that starts at the bottom and waits for morning (Psalm 130)
carry: more than watchmen for the morning

segments.voice: Yesterday: how long?, asked four times in a short psalm. Your line was but I have trusted. Did you say it once, honestly, about some waiting? Today, the end of the week, and a psalm that begins at the very bottom. Day seven hundred fourteen.

Four in the morning at a shut-up warehouse. The night guard walks the loading dock and looks east, over the rooftops. Still black. He finishes his round, pours coffee from a flask, looks east again. Still black. Somewhere a dog barks. Nobody on that shift can make the sun come up any faster. All anyone can do is keep watch, and look east, and wait. There's a psalm built exactly like that night.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING ON THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `THE EAST IS STILL BLACK.` → `A PSALM BUILT LIKE THAT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, from the bottom. Psalm one hundred thirty opens: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." No warm-up, no praise first. The singer is already down there, calling up. Second, no scorecard. Then a surprise: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared." If God kept a strict ledger, nobody would be left standing. And the psalm answers its own question: there is forgiveness. It's a different picture from the one Job's friends drew, where every suffering had a line in the ledger. Third, waiting for morning. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." The psalm says it twice, like someone looking east a second time. Another old translation puts it: more than watchmen for the morning. The watchmen can't hurry the dawn. They can only keep watch, sure it's coming. Fourth, the week. Look at what this week held. Job lost everything, and the reader knew it wasn't deserved. His friends sat seven days in silence, and then they talked, and were wrong. Job argued, and asked for a hearing. The whirlwind answered with stars and hawks. Psalm thirteen asked how long. And now this: a cry from the depths, and a long wait for the light. Not one of them explains suffering away. Each one finds a way to speak from inside it.
screen: `FROM THE BOTTOM.` · `NO SCORECARD.` · `WAITING FOR MORNING, TWICE.` · `A WEEK OF SPEAKING FROM INSIDE IT.` · then, large: `MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your weight sink down. Find the lowest place in you right now. It may be deep, or just a little low. Don't climb out of it yet. Instead, keep watch from there, the way the guard keeps watch. On each in-breath, look east, in your mind, toward where the light will come. On each out-breath, let the dark be dark a little longer. No forcing the dawn. If your attention wanders, come back and look east again, the way the psalm says its line a second time. The bell holds the time.
Watchmen, from Psalm one hundred thirty's ending: waiting for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, watchmen who cannot hurry the dawn. Today's word.

Your line: more than watchmen for the morning. Tomorrow at first light, or whenever you next see it, stop at a window or a doorway and watch the light arrive for one whole minute. Day seven hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 130, alone and in worship, and some people in both traditions turn to it in times of distress or grief.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Psalms are mostly happy hymns of praise.
what it means: Psalm 130 starts at the bottom, trusts in forgiveness, and waits for God like watchmen for the morning.
what a scholar hears: the doubled line about the watchmen (Psalm 130:6) is the psalm's own repetition, a wait spoken twice, before the psalm turns its hope outward to Israel (130:7–8).

notes: Editor: hook moved from a hospital ward to a night guard (hospital images already in days 710, 713 and 715); 'the ledger isn't how God works' (a narrator claim beyond the verse) now says only what 130:4 says, set beside Job's friends' picture; practice dropped the repeated 'if you pray... if not...' line.

The carry 'more than watchmen for the morning' (the index line) follows the wording of other translations, likely JPS 1917 ('more than watchmen for the morning'); the script says 'another old translation puts it' without quotation marks.
